notes.text:
The ledger did not stay closed. The accounts he settled that afternoon kept posting for another eighty years, and what they earned is the part of the story that has been erased. Tennessee Eastman, the subsidiary he had built to make his film base, operated the Y-12 plant at Oak Ridge for the Manhattan Project from 1943 to 1947, enriching the uranium for  the same  atomic bomb Kodak film had captured at the trinity test.
Kodak made the film that flew in the U-2 over the Soviet Union, and in October 1962 it was Kodak film that came back from Cuba, developed overnight in Washington and laid on Kennedy's desk showing Soviet missiles under canvas. The photograph as evidence at the highest table there is with the power to move navies. Kodak made the film for the satellites that replaced the U-2, whose capsules came out of orbit to be caught in midair by aircraft trailing hooks. One roll recovered in August 1960 covered more Soviet territory than every U-2 flight combined.

before.text: **The company ran for another eighty years on his instructions, and this is the part that has been erased.** Tennessee Eastman operated the uranium plant at Oak Ridge for the Manhattan Project. Kodak built the cameras that flew over the Soviet Union and made the film that came back to earth in canisters snatched out of the sky by aircraft trailing hooks. In 1966 a Kodak system developed film while in orbit around the moon and radioed home the first photograph of the Earth. For most of a century it was among the most trusted names on the planet, and it is now a slide in a deck about incumbents who fail to adapt.

notes.chunk_at_written: **The company ran for another eighty years on his instructions, and this is the part that has been erased.** Tennessee Eastman operated the Y-12 plant at Oak Ridge from 1943 to 1947 and enriched the uranium for. Kodak made the film for America's first spy satellites, whose capsules came back out of orbit to be caught in midair by aircraft trailing hooks, and built the cameras for the programs that followed. August 1966 a Kodak system orbiting the moon developed its own film on board, scanned the negatives, and radioed home the first photograph of the Earth. At its peak Kodak held ninety percent of the American film market and was the fourth most valuable brand on the planet. It is now a slide in a deck about incumbents who fail to adapt.
